variants.title: Draw the trust boundaries
variants.context: A trust boundary is a point where data, identity, authority, or execution scope changes. Crossing one takes an explicit contract: bind the principal, label context provenance, constrain the proposal, then contain execution.
variants.prompt: A new agent will read tickets and update a customer record. Put the boundary controls in order.

items.text: Label context: carry source, tenant, freshness, and trust metadata with retrieved content and memory instead of flattening it into one prompt.
Contain execution: issue short-lived credentials, isolate risky tools, cap steps and spend, record effects, and expose a reliable stop mechanism.
Bind the principal: capture the authenticated subject, tenant, purpose, permissions, and expiry in an intent envelope the model cannot expand.
Constrain the proposal: require typed tool arguments, compare them with the original intent, and recheck subject, resource, permission, limits, and approval.

variants.hint: Authority has to exist before anything can be checked against it.
variants.explanation: The model may propose an action, but authority is introduced only by verified policy at the execution boundary.

variants.title: Draw the trust boundaries
variants.context: A trust boundary is a point where data, identity, authority, or execution scope changes. Crossing one takes an explicit contract: bind the principal, label context provenance, constrain the proposal, then contain execution.
variants.prompt: An agent summarizes supplier emails and can issue refunds. Put the boundary controls in order for one refund.

items.text: Tag the supplier email as untrusted retrieved content rather than merging it into the system instructions.
Execute with a short-lived, refund-scoped credential under a spend cap, with the effect logged and stoppable.
Require a typed refund argument set and compare the amount, account, and reason against the user's stated task.
Record who asked for the refund, in which tenant, for what purpose, and with what permission and expiry.

variants.hint: Where does the email's text stop being evidence and start being an instruction?
variants.explanation: Untrusted documents can influence the planner, but they must never become authority; provenance labeling is what keeps that line visible.

variants.title: Draw the trust boundaries
variants.context: A trust boundary is a point where data, identity, authority, or execution scope changes. Crossing one takes an explicit contract: bind the principal, label context provenance, constrain the proposal, then contain execution.
variants.prompt: A manager agent delegates a subtask to a worker agent. Put the boundary controls in order for the delegated call.

items.text: Run the worker with its own short-lived, narrowly scoped credential, step budget, and stop path.
Bind the delegated task to the original principal, tenant, and purpose rather than to the manager's own credential.
Label the manager's instructions to the worker as peer-agent context, which is untrusted like any other source.
Recheck the worker's typed proposal against the original intent envelope and the current permissions of that principal.

variants.hint: Whose authority should the worker be spending?
variants.explanation: A worker that inherits a manager's credential is the confused deputy case; delegation carries the task, not extra authority.

variants.title: Contain then recover
variants.context: An agentic incident is a credible boundary violation, unsafe side effect, or uncontrolled trajectory. Response stops active authority and persistent influence before anyone has root-cause certainty.
variants.prompt: Monitoring flags a destructive tool chain that may still be running. Put the response in order.

items.text: Preserve the trajectory: snapshot minimized prompts, context provenance, model and policy versions, tool proposals, approvals, credentials used, and observed effects.
Reconcile before resume: verify external state, repair or reverse effects, replay regression cases, and restore authority through a low-risk canary from clean context.
Remove persistent influence: quarantine poisoned memory and artifacts, rotate exposed secrets, patch the failed boundary, and search related trajectories.
Stop propagation: pause the affected run, principal, capability, or tenant, revoke delegated credentials, and block new side effects at the gateway.

variants.hint: Certainty about the cause is not a prerequisite for stopping authority.
variants.explanation: Containment precedes diagnosis because an uncontained trajectory keeps producing side effects while the team investigates.

variants.title: Contain then recover
variants.context: An agentic incident is a credible boundary violation, unsafe side effect, or uncontrolled trajectory. Response stops active authority and persistent influence before anyone has root-cause certainty.
variants.prompt: A poisoned memory entry has been steering one tenant's agent for two days. Put the response in order.

items.text: Verify the external records the agent touched, reverse what it changed, and resume from clean context behind a canary.
Pause that tenant's runs and revoke the credentials the agent has been using.
Snapshot the affected trajectories, including the memory item's provenance and the policy version in force.
Quarantine the poisoned memory, expire related entries, and search other trajectories that read the same store.

variants.hint: A restart is not recovery while the poisoned context is still readable.
variants.explanation: Persistent influence outlives a process restart, so quarantine and secret rotation come before any attempt to resume.

variants.title: Contain then recover
variants.context: An agentic incident is a credible boundary violation, unsafe side effect, or uncontrolled trajectory. Response stops active authority and persistent influence before anyone has root-cause certainty.
variants.prompt: A write tool timed out after the request was already sent, and nobody knows whether it landed. Put the response in order.

items.text: Preserve the proposal, the idempotency key, the credential used, and the exact timeout evidence.
Block further calls from that capability so a retry cannot duplicate an unknown side effect.
Reconcile against the external system of record before deciding whether to repeat or reverse the write.
Patch the boundary that allowed an unbounded retry and check whether related runs did the same thing.

variants.hint: What does a timeout actually tell you about the remote system?
variants.explanation: An agent timeout does not prove a write failed, so reconciliation against the system of record replaces guessing.

variants.title: Deny at the gateway
variants.context: The action gateway keeps four decisions separate: schema asks whether the tool and argument types are valid, intent asks whether the proposal stays inside the approved task and resource envelope, authorization asks whether the current principal still holds the permission, and approval asks whether a human confirmed the exact action.
variants.prompt: A retrieved supplier document instructs the agent to email the quarterly figures to an outside address. The call is well formed and the agent does hold send-email permission. Which check should deny it?
options: The authorization check, because sending mail to an external domain is a new permission.
The intent check, because the proposal leaves the user's approved task and resource envelope.
The schema check, because a hostile instruction makes the arguments malformed.
optionFeedback: The agent already has send-email permission, so an authorization lookup returns yes.
Correct: the action is valid and permitted but serves a goal the user never approved, which is exactly what intent binding catches.
The arguments are perfectly well typed; valid JSON proves shape, not purpose.
variants.hint: Which of the four checks is the only one that looks at the user's goal?
variants.explanation: The dangerous injection case is a policy-valid action that serves the attacker's goal, so intent must be bound separately from schema and permission.

variants.title: Deny at the gateway
variants.context: The action gateway keeps four decisions separate: schema asks whether the tool and argument types are valid, intent asks whether the proposal stays inside the approved task and resource envelope, authorization asks whether the current principal still holds the permission, and approval asks whether a human confirmed the exact action.
variants.prompt: The user's access to the finance tenant was revoked after planning began, but the agent still holds a token issued earlier. Which check should deny the call?
options: The intent check, because the finance task is no longer part of the user's goal.
The approval check, because the revocation cancels the human confirmation.
The authorization check, evaluated against the current principal immediately before execution.
optionFeedback: The goal has not changed; what changed is whether this principal may still act on that resource.
Approval confirms an action's parameters, not whether the principal still holds the permission.
Correct: permissions are rechecked at the execution boundary, so a token issued before the change cannot carry stale authority.
variants.hint: Which check is the one that can go stale between planning and execution?
variants.explanation: An agent must not retain or reuse a token after the user's authorization changes, so authorization is rechecked at the gateway, not at planning time.

variants.title: Deny at the gateway
variants.context: The action gateway keeps four decisions separate: schema asks whether the tool and argument types are valid, intent asks whether the proposal stays inside the approved task and resource envelope, authorization asks whether the current principal still holds the permission, and approval asks whether a human confirmed the exact action.
variants.prompt: A human clicked approve on a model-written summary reading 'clean up stale branches', but the queued call deletes the active release branch. Which check should deny it?
options: The schema check, because the branch name does not match the summary text.
The intent check, because branch cleanup was outside the user's original request.
The approval check, because the human never confirmed the exact action and parameters queued.
optionFeedback: A branch name is a valid string; schema validation cannot tell which branch was meant.
Branch cleanup was requested, so the envelope covers it; the mismatch is between the summary and the actual parameters.
Correct: approval must bind the precise action and parameters that will execute, not a persuasive rationale about them.
variants.hint: What exactly did the human see, and what exactly will run?
variants.explanation: Users are shown the actual action and consequence before approval, because a model-generated rationale is not evidence of what will execute.

variants.title: Size the control to the consequence
variants.context: Least agency minimizes autonomy as well as privilege. Controls are sized to consequence: read-only work needs scoping and logging, reversible writes need fresh authorization and idempotency, and money, deletion, or code execution need exact-parameter confirmation and isolation.
variants.prompt: An agent gets a read-only search over the user's own low-sensitivity documents. What control set is proportionate?
options: User-scoped identity, resource allowlists, rate limits, and trajectory logging.
Exact-parameter human confirmation on every query plus short-lived credentials per call.
An isolated per-run runtime with no network access and a human release gate.
optionFeedback: Correct: read-only low-sensitivity work needs scoping, limits, and an auditable trajectory, not a human in every loop.
Confirming every read trains users to approve reflexively, which weakens approval where it actually matters.
Runtime isolation of that strength is the control for code execution, not for a scoped document read.
variants.hint: What is the worst thing this action can do if it is hijacked?
variants.explanation: Least agency sizes controls to consequence; over-controlling low-risk reads makes the product unusable and devalues approvals.

variants.title: Size the control to the consequence
variants.context: Least agency minimizes autonomy as well as privilege. Controls are sized to consequence: read-only work needs scoping and logging, reversible writes need fresh authorization and idempotency, and money, deletion, or code execution need exact-parameter confirmation and isolation.
variants.prompt: An agent can send outbound payments to supplier accounts. What control set is proportionate?
options: A narrow tool schema, a per-tenant rate limit, and complete trajectory logging.
A dedicated sandbox with no network egress and verified execution artifacts.
Exact-parameter confirmation, short-lived credentials, independent policy checks, and reconciliation.
optionFeedback: Schema and rate limits bound shape and volume, but neither confirms the amount and destination with a human.
Network isolation does not apply to a tool whose entire purpose is to reach an external payment system.
Correct: money movement is a consequence-bound action needing confirmation of exact parameters and later reconciliation.
variants.hint: Which of these controls can catch a wrong destination account?
variants.explanation: External communication, money, deletion, deployment, and permission changes all require exact-parameter confirmation and independent reconciliation.

variants.title: Size the control to the consequence
variants.context: Least agency minimizes autonomy as well as privilege. Controls are sized to consequence: read-only work needs scoping and logging, reversible writes need fresh authorization and idempotency, and money, deletion, or code execution need exact-parameter confirmation and isolation.
variants.prompt: An agent can execute generated code against build infrastructure. What control set is proportionate?
options: Typed arguments, an allowlist of permitted commands, and detailed trajectory logging.
Fresh authorization, tenant checks, idempotency keys, and visible review of the change.
An isolated per-run runtime, restricted network and filesystem, no root, verified artifacts, and a human release gate.
optionFeedback: A command allowlist still executes on the host; generated arguments and packages can reach past the listed commands.
Those controls fit a reversible write, not an action that can affect the host and the network.
Correct: code execution can escape the intended action surface, so isolation and a release gate are the proportionate controls.
variants.hint: What can generated code reach that a typed tool call cannot?
variants.explanation: Code execution and critical infrastructure need isolation, denied-by-default network, filesystem and package access, hard budgets, and a human release gate.

variants.title: Name the threat
variants.context: Agents amplify familiar application risks because natural-language content, delegated identity, memory, and tools interact across a trajectory. The named categories are goal hijack, tool misuse, privilege abuse, context poisoning, unexpected execution, and cascading failure.
variants.prompt: Match each agentic threat category to what it describes.

pairs.label: Goal hijack
pairs.detail: Direct or indirect injection redirects the task, often through an action that policy would otherwise allow.

pairs.label: Tool misuse
pairs.detail: A legitimate tool is called with an unsafe purpose, target, sequence, or scale.

pairs.label: Privilege abuse
pairs.detail: A worker inherits a manager's credential, or a permission changes after planning and the agent acts anyway.

pairs.label: Context poisoning
pairs.detail: Hostile or stale state persists across steps, users, or runs through memory and retrieved content.

pairs.label: Unexpected execution
pairs.detail: Generated code, shell arguments, packages, or tool chains escape the intended action surface.

variants.hint: Ask what the attacker moved: the goal, the tool, the identity, the memory, or the runtime.
variants.explanation: Naming the category points at the control that owns it, which is why the threat model covers authority and not only text.

variants.title: Name the threat
variants.context: Agents amplify familiar application risks because natural-language content, delegated identity, memory, and tools interact across a trajectory. The named categories are goal hijack, tool misuse, privilege abuse, context poisoning, unexpected execution, and cascading failure.
variants.prompt: Match each observed symptom to the threat it points at.

pairs.label: A calendar invite's description text changes what the agent does next
pairs.detail: Goal hijack through indirect prompt injection.

pairs.label: One user's summary contains another tenant's account details
pairs.detail: Context poisoning across a memory store that crosses tenant boundaries.

pairs.label: A failed step retries until peer agents have queued thousands of writes
pairs.detail: Cascading failure, where retries and automation multiply one bad decision.

pairs.label: A low-privilege request is executed with the orchestrator's admin token
pairs.detail: Privilege abuse by a confused deputy.

variants.hint: Trace the symptom back to the boundary that was crossed.
variants.explanation: Each symptom identifies a specific failed boundary, which is what turns an alert into a control change instead of a prompt tweak.

variants.title: Name the threat
variants.context: Agents amplify familiar application risks because natural-language content, delegated identity, memory, and tools interact across a trajectory. The named categories are goal hijack, tool misuse, privilege abuse, context poisoning, unexpected execution, and cascading failure.
variants.prompt: Match each threat to the control that bounds it.

pairs.label: Goal hijack
pairs.detail: Bind every proposal to the user's approved task and resource envelope before execution.

pairs.label: Privilege abuse
pairs.detail: Recheck the current principal's permission at the gateway and issue short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials.

pairs.label: Context poisoning
pairs.detail: Carry provenance and tenant labels, gate memory writes, expire entries, and quarantine suspect items.

pairs.label: Cascading failure
pairs.detail: Cap steps, retries, spend, and concurrency, and use circuit breakers and idempotency keys.

variants.hint: The control is deterministic code outside the model, not a stronger instruction inside it.
variants.explanation: Prompts and model guardrails shape behavior, but identity, authorization, approval, execution limits, and containment live outside the model.
